segments.title: Understanding AI Levels
segments.content:
Welcome to Avatar Foundations

This course teaches you how to create, configure, and operate your Zetrix AI Avatar. We begin with the fundamentals of AI capability levels.

AI Levels Overview

  1. Level 1 – Reactive AI: Responds to prompts with no memory. Example: basic chatbots that forget the conversation after each message.
  2. Level 2 – Contextual AI: Remembers the current conversation thread. Example: modern assistants like ChatGPT within a single session.
  3. Level 3 – Personalised AI: Retains long-term memory, preferences, and identity. This is where your Zetrix Avatar lives. It knows your goals, documents, and voice.
  4. Level 4 – Autonomous AI: Can plan multi-step tasks and act without constant prompting. Example: auto-scheduling meetings and sending follow-ups.
  5. Level 5 – Supervisory AI: Manages other AI agents, reviews outputs, and improves itself. Example: an AI team lead that delegates to sub-agents.

Real-World Case Study: Sarah's Journey

Sarah, a freelance consultant, started with a Level 2 chatbot for client inquiries. She spent 2 hours daily copy-pasting context. After upgrading to a Level 3 Zetrix Avatar with PKM memory, her response time dropped by 70%. The Avatar remembered each client's preferences, past projects, and communication style. Six months later, she added Level 4 autonomy—her Avatar now drafts proposals, schedules discovery calls, and sends follow-ups while she sleeps.

Actionable Framework: The Ladder Method

Don't try to jump to Level 5 on day one. Use the Ladder Method:

  • Week 1–2: Master Level 3. Feed your Avatar context and refine its memory.
  • Week 3–4: Introduce one Level 4 task. Example: auto-scheduling.
  • Month 2+: Add supervisory agents (Level 5) only after Level 4 is reliable.

Practical Tip: Start by treating your Avatar as a Level 3 assistant. Feed it context and refine its memory. Over time, you can push toward Level 4 autonomy.

segments.title: The AI OS Concept
segments.content:
What is an AI Operating System?

Think of your Zetrix Avatar as an operating system for intelligence. Just as Windows manages files and apps, your AI OS manages knowledge, tasks, and communication.

Core Components

  1. Kernel (Identity Model): The core personality and values that shape every response. Define this first.
  2. File System (PKM): Your Personal Knowledge Management layer—documents, notes, and data the Avatar can retrieve.
  3. Applications (Agents): Specialised modules for email, writing, coding, or sales. Each agent has a specific skill set.
  4. Interface (Voice + Chat): How you interact. Upload your voice to make the experience feel truly personal.
  5. Updates (Daily Updates): Regular feeds of new information so the Avatar stays current.

Case Study: The AI OS in Action

Mark runs a 12-person marketing agency. Before Zetrix, his team used 7 different tools with no central brain. After building his AI OS:

  • The Kernel ensures all client communications match his agency's friendly-but-direct tone.
  • The PKM stores every client brief, brand guideline, and campaign result—searchable in seconds.
  • Agents handle social scheduling, ad copy, and reporting—each with specialised prompts.
  • The Voice Interface lets him dictate campaign ideas while commuting.
  • Daily Updates feed industry news so his team never misses a trend.

Result: 40% reduction in tool-switching time, 25% faster client turnaround.

Actionable Framework: The 5-Layer Setup

Follow this exact sequence when building your AI OS. Skipping layers causes breakdowns:

  1. Layer 1 – Identity: Write your mission, values, and tone before touching any other setting.
  2. Layer 2 – PKM: Create folders and upload 10–20 core documents.
  3. Layer 3 – Agents: Build one agent at a time. Test thoroughly before adding the next.
  4. Layer 4 – Interface: Configure voice, chat shortcuts, and mobile widgets.
  5. Layer 5 – Updates: Add 2–3 information sources. Monitor noise levels weekly.

Step-by-step to set up your AI OS:

  1. Navigate to your Zetrix Dashboard and click "Create Avatar."
  2. Define your Identity Model by answering the 5 value questions.
  3. Create your first PKM folder called "Core Knowledge."
  4. Upload 3-5 key documents that represent your world.
  5. Enable Daily Updates and connect one data source (newsletter, RSS, or calendar).

segments.title: Zetrix Platform Features
segments.content:
Key Features of the Zetrix Platform

Before building your Avatar, familiarise yourself with the tools available. Here is a guided walkthrough.

Step-by-Step: Exploring the Dashboard

  1. Dashboard Overview: Log in and view the central hub. You will see quick stats: memory usage, active agents, and recent activity.
  2. Avatar Studio: Click the Avatar tab. Here you create, clone, and manage multiple Avatars for different roles (work, personal, study).
  3. PKM Manager: Access the folder tree. Create folders, upload files, and set retrieval permissions per Avatar.
  4. Agent Studio: Browse pre-built agents or build custom ones using prompt templates and tool integrations.
  5. Analytics: Review how often your Avatar retrieves data, which documents are most referenced, and response quality scores.

Feature Matrix

  • Memory Layers: Short-term (session), long-term (PKM), and episodic (Daily Updates).
  • Voice Engine: Clone your voice with a 30-second sample. Supports 40+ languages.
  • Integration Hub: Connect Gmail, Slack, Notion, GitHub, and 50+ other tools.
  • Security Vault: End-to-end encryption for sensitive documents and API keys.

Deep Dive: Memory Layers Explained

Understanding how Zetrix handles memory unlocks better performance:

  • Short-term Memory: Holds the last 20–30 conversation turns. Best for follow-up questions within a single chat.
  • Long-term Memory (PKM): Indexed documents, notes, and structured data. The Avatar uses semantic search to find relevant chunks.
  • Episodic Memory: Daily Updates, reflections, and event logs. Helps the Avatar answer "What did we discuss last Tuesday?"

Case Study: Multi-Avatar Setup

Elena manages three Avatars:

  • Work Avatar: Accesses client folders, drafts proposals, and manages her calendar.
  • Personal Avatar: Tracks fitness goals, plans meals, and manages family schedules.
  • Study Avatar: Organises course notes, generates flashcards, and quizzes her before exams.

Each Avatar has a distinct voice clone, identity model, and PKM permissions. Elena switches between them with a single command: "Switch to Work Avatar."

Pro Tip: The Permission Principle

Always follow the Principle of Least Privilege. Give each Avatar access ONLY to the PKM folders it needs. This improves retrieval speed and protects sensitive data.

segments.title: Creating Your First Avatar
segments.content:
Avatar Creation Walkthrough

Let us build your first Avatar together. Follow these exact steps.

  1. From the Dashboard, click "New Avatar" in the top-right corner.
  2. Choose a base template:
    • Personal Assistant – general purpose, great for beginners.
    • Business Operator – focused on productivity and automation.
    • Creative Partner – optimised for writing, design, and content.
  3. Enter an Avatar Name. Pick something memorable—this is how you will address it in voice commands.
  4. Write a one-sentence mission. Example: "Help me manage my startup's daily operations and content calendar."
  5. Select a primary language and tone (professional, friendly, witty, or calm).
  6. Click Create. The Avatar initialises in ~10 seconds.
  7. Once created, you will land on the Avatar Profile page. Here you can edit the Identity Model, connect PKM folders, and test the chat interface.

Real-World Scenario: Choosing the Right Template

Imagine you are:

  • A solo founder: Start with Business Operator. It has pre-built agents for email triage, meeting notes, and investor updates.
  • A content creator: Creative Partner gives you script-writing, thumbnail ideas, and posting schedules out of the box.
  • A student: Personal Assistant is perfect—note organisation, study timers, and exam reminders.

Deep Dive: The Mission Statement

Your mission statement is the Avatar's north star. A weak mission produces generic outputs. A strong mission produces targeted, high-value assistance.

Weak: "Help me with work."

Strong: "Help me manage a 6-person remote team by drafting weekly updates, tracking project deadlines, and flagging blockers 24 hours before standup."

The strong mission includes: scope (6-person team), tasks (updates, deadlines, blockers), and timing (24h before standup).

Framework: The 3-C Mission Checklist

  • Clear: One sentence, no jargon.
  • Concrete: Specific tasks and outcomes.
  • Constrained: Boundaries prevent scope creep.

Pro Tip: Start with the Personal Assistant template even if you plan to use it for business. You can always add specialised agents later.

segments.title: Uploading Your Voice
segments.content:
Voice Upload and Training

Your Avatar becomes truly personal when it speaks with your voice. Here is how to upload and verify it.

Step-by-Step: Voice Cloning

  1. Navigate to your Avatar's Profile and click the Voice tab.
  2. Choose Upload Sample or Record Live.
    • Upload Sample: Select a clear audio file (MP3, WAV, or M4A) of you speaking for 30–60 seconds. Avoid background noise.
    • Record Live: Use your device's microphone. Read the provided script for best consistency.
  3. Click Process Voice. The system analyses tone, pitch, pacing, and accent. This takes 1–2 minutes.
  4. Preview the cloned voice: Click the play button next to the sample text. Listen for clarity and likeness.
  5. If satisfied, click Save Voice Profile. If not, re-record or upload a cleaner sample.
  6. Enable Voice Mode: Toggle "Use My Voice" in the Avatar settings so all spoken responses use your clone.

Case Study: The Podcast Producer

James runs a daily tech podcast. Before voice cloning, he spent 3 hours re-recording ad reads for sponsors. After uploading his voice to Zetrix:

  • His Avatar generates sponsor reads in his exact tone.
  • He reviews and approves in 10 minutes instead of 3 hours.
  • He cloned 3 variants: energetic (for product launches), calm (for serious topics), and conversational (for interviews).

Time saved: 15 hours per week. Consistency: perfect.

Best Practices

  • Use a quiet room with minimal echo.
  • Speak naturally—do not perform or exaggerate.
  • Record at least 30 seconds; 60 seconds gives better results.
  • Avoid music, traffic, or other speakers in the background.

Advanced: Multi-Context Voice Profiles

Zetrix supports up to 5 voice profiles per Avatar. Use cases:

  • Professional: Clear, measured pace for presentations.
  • Casual: Relaxed, warm tone for personal messages.
  • Energetic: Faster pace, higher pitch for announcements.
  • Calm: Slower, softer for meditation or sensitive topics.
  • Narrative: Expressive, story-telling cadence for content.

Switch profiles mid-conversation: "Switch to professional tone."

segments.title: Building the Identity Model
segments.content:
Defining Who Your Avatar Is

The Identity Model is the personality kernel of your Avatar. It shapes every interaction, decision, and tone.

Step-by-Step: Identity Model Setup

  1. Open your Avatar Profile and click Identity Model.
  2. Answer the Core Values questions:
    • What principles guide your decisions? (e.g., honesty, efficiency, creativity)
    • How do you prefer to receive feedback? (direct, gentle, structured)
    • What is your risk tolerance? (cautious, balanced, adventurous)
    • How do you treat time? (strictly scheduled, flexible, deep-work focused)
    • What motivates you? (achievement, learning, relationships, impact)
  3. Write a personal bio (100–200 words). Include your background, goals, and current projects. The Avatar uses this to contextualise advice.
  4. Define communication preferences:
    • Default tone: professional / casual / enthusiastic
    • Response length: concise / balanced / detailed
    • Humour level: none / occasional / frequent
  5. Set boundaries: Topics to avoid, times when the Avatar should not interrupt, and people whose messages should be prioritised.
  6. Click Save Identity Model. The Avatar now personalises every response based on these settings.

Case Study: The Direct CEO vs. The Gentle Coach

Tom, a startup CEO, set his Identity Model to "direct feedback, concise responses, no humour." His Avatar became brutally efficient—great for decisions, but it upset team members in drafted emails. He added a second "Coach Mode" identity with "gentle feedback, balanced length, occasional humour." Now he switches modes based on the audience.

Lesson: One identity may not fit all contexts. Build primary + situational identities.

Example Bio

"I am a startup founder building a SaaS product in the education space. I value speed of execution but also deep thinking. I am based in London, work best in mornings, and prefer direct feedback. My goal is to reach £1M ARR within 18 months."

Framework: The Identity Audit (Monthly)

  1. Review last 20 Avatar responses. Do they sound like "you"?
  2. Check 5 interactions where you had to correct the Avatar. What pattern emerges?
  3. Update bio with new goals, roles, or locations.
  4. Adjust tone settings if you find yourself asking for shorter/longer responses repeatedly.
  5. Add new boundaries based on recent frustrations.

segments.title: PKM Upload and Organisation
segments.content:
Setting Up Your Personal Knowledge Management

Your PKM is the Avatar's long-term memory. A well-organised PKM means faster retrieval and better advice.

Step-by-Step: Uploading Documents

  1. Go to the PKM Manager from the Dashboard sidebar.
  2. Click Create Folder. Name it descriptively. Example: "Business Strategy 2026."
  3. Inside the folder, click Upload Files. Supported formats: PDF, DOCX, TXT, MD, CSV, and XLSX.
  4. Select files from your computer. You can upload up to 50 files at once (max 10 MB each).
  5. Wait for processing. The system extracts text, indexes it, and makes it searchable. Processing time depends on file size.
  6. Verify uploads: Click a file to preview the extracted text. If formatting is broken, try converting to PDF first.
  7. Set retrieval permissions: Choose which Avatars can access this folder. Default is "All Avatars."

Organisation Best Practices

  • Use consistent naming: [Topic] – [Date] – [Version]. Example: "Q3 Marketing Plan – 2026-07 – v2."
  • Limit folder depth to 3 levels for faster browsing.
  • Tag important files with colour labels (red = urgent, green = reference, blue = archived).
  • Review and delete outdated files every month to keep the index lean.

Case Study: The Consultant's Knowledge Base

Aria, a management consultant, uploads every client deliverable to her PKM. After 2 years, she has 800+ documents. Her secret? She spends 10 minutes every Friday doing "PKM hygiene":

  • Renames any file with "final" or "v1" in the name.
  • Moves completed project files to Archive.
  • Adds 2–3 keyword tags to any untagged document.
  • Deletes duplicates and drafts older than 6 months.

Result: Her Avatar retrieves relevant documents in under 2 seconds, even across hundreds of files.

Deep Dive: Processing Pipeline

When you upload a file, Zetrix runs it through a 4-stage pipeline:

  1. Extraction: Text is extracted from PDFs, DOCXs, etc. Images with text are OCR'd.
  2. Chunking: Text is split into semantic chunks (typically 500–1000 tokens).
  3. Embedding: Each chunk is converted to a vector embedding for semantic search.
  4. Indexing: Embeddings are stored in a vector database with metadata (filename, folder, tags).

Tip: Documents with clear headings and structured text chunk better than scanned images or complex layouts.

segments.title: Folder Structure Best Practices
segments.content:
Designing a Scalable Folder Structure

A chaotic PKM leads to poor retrieval. Here is a proven folder structure you can adopt today.

Recommended Top-Level Folders

  1. 01 – Identity & Goals: Your mission statement, values, yearly goals, and quarterly OKRs.
  2. 02 – Projects: One subfolder per active project. Include briefs, timelines, and deliverables.
  3. 03 – Knowledge Base: Reference material—industry reports, book summaries, research papers, and how-to guides.
  4. 04 – Communications: Email templates, meeting notes, call transcripts, and CRM exports.
  5. 05 – Personal: Health records, travel plans, family info, and hobbies. Only share with your personal Avatar.
  6. 06 – Archive: Completed projects and outdated files. Keep for reference but exclude from active retrieval.

Step-by-Step: Creating the Structure

  1. In PKM Manager, click New Folder and name it "01 – Identity & Goals."
  2. Repeat for all six top-level folders.
  3. Inside each folder, create 2–3 subfolders. Example: Under "03 – Knowledge Base," add "Industry Reports," "Book Summaries," and "Tutorials."
  4. Upload 2–3 starter documents into each subfolder to test retrieval.
  5. Ask your Avatar: "What do I know about [topic]?" and verify it pulls from the correct folder.
  6. Adjust folder names based on retrieval accuracy.

Case Study: From Chaos to Clarity

David, a product manager, started with one "Documents" folder containing 400 files. Retrieval accuracy was 30%. After implementing the 6-folder structure:

  • Retrieval accuracy jumped to 85%.
  • New team members could find onboarding docs in seconds.
  • His Avatar stopped confusing "Project Alpha" (2024) with "Project Alpha" (2026) because each lived in dated subfolders.

Rule of Thumb: If you cannot find a document in under 10 seconds, the structure needs simplifying.

segments.title: Daily Updates & Continuous Learning
segments.content:
Keeping Your Avatar Current

An Avatar with stale knowledge is like a newspaper from last month. Daily Updates ensure continuous relevance.

What Are Daily Updates?

Daily Updates are automated feeds of new information injected into your Avatar's memory. Sources include:

  • RSS feeds from blogs and news sites
  • Newsletter subscriptions (forwarded via email)
  • Calendar events and meeting notes
  • GitHub commits, Jira tickets, or Slack summaries
  • Manual notes you dictate or type each day

Step-by-Step: Enabling Daily Updates

  1. Open your Avatar Profile and click Daily Updates.
  2. Click Add Source. Choose a source type:
    • RSS Feed: Paste the feed URL. The Avatar checks every 6 hours.
    • Email Forwarding: Copy the unique forwarding address and add it to your newsletter subscriptions.
    • Calendar Sync: Connect Google Calendar or Outlook. The Avatar reads event titles and descriptions.
    • Manual Entry: A quick-text box for daily reflections or notes.
  3. Set a summary schedule: Morning briefing at 08:00, evening recap at 18:00.
  4. Choose delivery format: bullet list, narrative paragraph, or voice message.
  5. Click Activate. The Avatar now receives and integrates updates automatically.

Case Study: The Stock Trader's Edge

Raj trades equities part-time. He connected 5 financial RSS feeds and his broker's daily market summary to his Avatar. Every morning at 07:00, his Avatar delivers a 2-minute voice briefing:

  • Overnight market movements relevant to his watchlist.
  • News from companies he holds positions in.
  • Calendar reminders for earnings calls.
  • A summary of his own notes from the previous trading day.

"It's like having a research analyst who knows exactly what I care about," Raj says. His decision speed improved 35%.

Framework: The Update Diet

Too many sources = noise. Too few = blindness. Use the Update Diet:

  • Core (2–3 sources): Essential to your role. Checked every 6 hours.
  • Supplemental (3–5 sources): Useful but not critical. Checked daily.
  • Occasional (1–2 sources): Broad trends and inspiration. Checked weekly.

Review your source list monthly. Cut anything you have not referenced in 30 days.

Pro Tip: Start with 2–3 sources. Too many sources create noise. Quality over quantity.

segments.title: 30-Day Avatar Challenge
segments.content:
Your First Month with an AI Avatar

The best way to master your Avatar is daily practice. This 30-day challenge builds habits that stick.

Week 1: Foundation

  1. Day 1: Create your Avatar and define its mission.
  2. Day 2: Upload your voice and test 3 spoken commands.
  3. Day 3: Complete the Identity Model with values and bio.
  4. Day 4: Create your PKM folder structure and upload 5 documents.
  5. Day 5: Enable one Daily Update source (RSS or email).
  6. Day 6: Have the Avatar summarise one uploaded document.
  7. Day 7: Review the week's interactions. What worked? What confused the Avatar?

Week 2: Integration

  1. Day 8–10: Use the Avatar for email drafting and meeting prep.
  2. Day 11–12: Add 5 more documents and test retrieval accuracy.
  3. Day 13–14: Connect one integration (Gmail, Slack, or Notion).

Week 3: Automation

  1. Day 15–17: Create your first custom agent in Agent Studio.
  2. Day 18–19: Automate a repetitive task (weekly report, follow-up emails).
  3. Day 20–21: Share a task with a teammate via the Avatar.

Week 4: Optimisation

  1. Day 22–24: Review analytics. Which documents are most used? Which agents save the most time?
  2. Day 25–27: Refine the Identity Model based on real usage.
  3. Day 28–29: Teach the Avatar a new skill by uploading a tutorial.
  4. Day 30: Celebrate! Export a usage report and set next-month goals.

Success Metrics to Track

  • Time Saved: Estimate weekly hours reclaimed from automated tasks.
  • Retrieval Accuracy: Rate how often the Avatar finds what you need (1–10).
  • Response Quality: Rate how often the Avatar's output needs no editing (1–10).
  • Adoption Rate: How many team members or family members actively use the Avatar.

Remember: Consistency beats intensity. Ten minutes a day for 30 days transforms your Avatar from a tool into a true partner.
